Keywords Glial cell line-derived neurotrophic factor GDNF Meta-analysis Schizophrenia pmc-status-qastatus 0 pmc-status-live yes pmc-status-embargo no pmc-status-released yes pmc-prop-open-access yes pmc-prop-olf no pmc-prop-manuscript no pmc-prop-legally-suppressed no pmc-prop-has-pdf yes pmc-prop-has-supplement yes pmc-prop-pdf-only no pmc-prop-suppress-copyright no pmc-prop-is-real-version no pmc-prop-is-scanned-article no pmc-prop-preprint no pmc-prop-in-epmc yes pmc-license-ref CC BY issue-copyright-statement © BioMed Central Ltd., part of Springer Nature 2025 Background Schizophrenia (SCZ) is one of the most prevalent functional psychiatric disorder, characterized by a range of symptoms including hallucinations, slurred speech, delusions, and impaired cognitive function [ 1 ]. Approximately 20 million individuals worldwide are affected by this disorder, with prevalence rates increasing significantly by 65.85% from 1990 to 2019 [ 2 , 3 ]. Despite decades of research, the underlying causes of SCZ remain largely elusive, complicating the establishment of definitive diagnostic criteria and a comprehensive understanding of its pathophysiology. These challenges have hindered efforts to develop effective treatments [ 4 ]. Risk factors for SCZ are generally classified into genetic, environmental, psychosocial, developmental, and biological domains [ 5 ]. Among these biological factors, neurotrophic factors—particularly glial cell line-derived neurotrophic factor (GDNF)—are critical for elucidating the pathophysiology of SCZ [ 6 – 12 ]. GDNF plays a crucial role in the nervous system by promoting the survival, differentiation, and function of dopaminergic neurons, which are essential for normal brain activity [ 13 ]. It primarily exerts its effects through interactions with the GDNF family receptor-α1, leading to the activation of Ret tyrosine kinase receptors. This signaling cascade is vital for several key processes, including neuronal survival, neurite outgrowth, and synaptogenesis—each of which contributes to the maintenance of healthy neural networks [ 14 ]. In addition to its role in neurodevelopment, GDNF has demonstrated significant neuroprotective effects in various experimental models. For instance, it helps preserve neuron-glial networks under hypoxic conditions and regulates the expression of hypoxia-inducible factor 1-alpha (HIF-1α) [ 15 ]. The neuroprotective actions of GDNF are mediated through several intracellular pathways, notably the RET kinase receptor complex and the PI3K/Akt signaling pathway [ 16 – 18 ]. These pathways are critical for supporting neuronal health and functionality by promoting cell survival and mitigating cellular stress. Several studies have reported associations between GDNF levels and various mental disorders, including mood disorders [ 19 ], anxiety [ 20 ], depression [ 21 ], and bipolar disorder [ 22 ]. Notably, alterations in GDNF levels have been observed in patients with major depressive disorder [ 21 ] and bipolar disorder [ 22 ], suggesting a potential role for GDNF in the pathophysiology of these conditions. However, the role of GDNF as a biomarker in psychiatric disorders—particularly SCZ—remains a topic of ongoing debate. While GDNF is crucial for the survival and function of dopaminergic neurons [ 13 ], its precise role in the pathophysiology of SCZ has yet to be fully elucidated. Research on serum levels of GDNF in schizophrenia reveals several critical gaps. While some studies indicate lower GDNF levels in patients with SCZ [ 6 – 12 , 23 , 24 ], others report no significant differences or higher levels [ 25 – 27 ]. These heterogeneous results highlight the need for larger standardized studies. Additionally, associations between GDNF and clinical symptoms remain preliminary and require validation across diverse populations. Furthermore, the biological mechanisms linking GDNF to schizophrenia are poorly understood. There is also insufficient exploration of how comorbid conditions may influence GDNF levels. Our current understanding is limited to original studies that do not adequately address differences between sociodemographic subgroups or consider how sample size and study quality impact findings. Addressing these gaps could enhance our understanding of GDNF's role in schizophrenia and improve diagnostic and therapeutic approaches. The primary aim of this meta-analysis is to calculate a pooled estimate of circulating levels of GDNF in patients with SCZ compared to healthy controls. By synthesizing data from existing studies, we seek to clarify the inconsistencies in reported GDNF levels and their potential associations with clinical symptoms. To achieve our secondary objectives, we conducted subgroup and meta-regression analyses to assess the impact of several sociodemographic and clinical factors—including geographic region, sex ratio, age of illness onset, disease duration, daily dose of Chlorpromazine, and total score of the Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale (PANSS), study year, and study quality-on GDNF levels. This comprehensive approach aims to enhance our understanding of GDNF's role in schizophrenia and its potential as a biomarker for diagnosis and treatment. Methods Search strategy and databases This study conducted a systematic search across PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, and ScienceDirect. Our systematic review and meta-analysis were carried out following the methodological steps outlined in the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines, registered in PROSPERO by code CRD42024576318 and at Kermanshah University of Medical Sciences, Kermanshah, Iran (ethical approval number: IR.KUMS.REC.1403.401). Two authors (F.K. and M.M.) independently searched from the first date available up to 17 June 2024. We used the key search terms according to the PICOS formula [ 28 ]: ((schizophrenia[Title/Abstract]) OR (schizophrenia[MeSH Terms])) AND (((GDNF[Title/Abstract]) OR (glial cell line-derived neurotrophic factor[MeSH Terms])) OR (glial cell line-derived neurotrophic factor[Title/Abstract])) in PubMed, obtaining 51 articles. We also used the key search terms: (TITLE-ABS-KEY (GDNF) OR TITLE-ABS-KEY ("glial cell line-derived neurotrophic factor") AND TITLE-ABS-KEY (schizophrenia)) in Scopus, obtaining 171 articles. Additionally, we searched for (glial cell line-derived neurotrophic factor" or GDNF and schizophrenia) in Science Direct, obtaining 16 articles. We used the search terms: ((TS = (GDNF)) OR TS = ("glial cell line-derived neurotrophic factor ")) AND TS = (schizophrenia) in the Web of Science, obtaining 81 articles. Selection criteria The inclusion criteria were as follows: 1) patients with SCZ, 2) healthy control subjects without current mental disorder, 3) a reported GDNF levels in serum, 4) adults 18 years of age or older, regardless of gender, 5) case–control studies, and 6) clinical trials and cohort studies if reporting baseline data. The studies were excluded based on the following criteria: 1) animal or in vitro studies, 2) reviews or meta-analyses except for manual search of their references, 3) studies focused on genetic polymorphism or gene expression, 4) studies lacking a control group of healthy individuals, and 5) abstracts without full text. Screening of studies Data were extracted by two independent researchers (F.K. and M.M.). After extraction, both researchers compared their data and, in the case of any discrepancies, collaborated to reach a consensus to ensure that the extracted data were accurate and valid. All the search results were imported into EndNote v20. After eliminating duplicates, two authors independently reviewed the titles, abstracts, and full texts of the potentially eligible articles. In cases of disagreement between the two authors, the third author (O.D.) was consulted to resolve the matter. A total of 319 studies were identified through electronic searches. After eliminating duplicates, 199 articles were retained. A review of the titles and abstracts of these articles resulted in the exclusion of 180 articles. Consequently, 20 articles were selected for full-text evaluation. Following this evaluation, 8 articles were excluded, resulting in a total of 12 articles published between 2014 and 2023 being included in the meta-analysis. Figure 1 illustrates the PRISMA flow diagram. Fig. 1 PRISMA flow diagram of the study procedure Extraction of data The variables extracted from the studies included: 1) mean and standard deviation of the GDNF levels for each group, 2) the number of patients and controls, 3) age and gender of patients and controls, 4) scores in PANSS scales in patients, 5) the mean dose of Chlorpromazine equivalents used by patients (mg), 6) duration of treatment in patient group, 7) characteristics of measurement (ELISA kit utilized), 8) study design (case–control, cohort and cross-sectional), and 9) age of onset of illness. When a study measured GDNF blood levels at two different time points [ 7 , 9 , 24 , 27 ], we used the GDNF levels at the baseline period. In some studies that report the median GDNF levels [ 12 , 23 ], we calculated the mean and standard deviation of the GDNF levels using other parameters explained by researchers [ 29 ]. In two studies, SCZ patients were categorized into two groups, with GDNF values reported separately for each group. The combined mean was then utilized to derive the final values for both groups [ 6 , 24 ]. Evaluation of quality The methodological quality of the studies was evaluated using the Newcastle–Ottawa Scale (NOS) specifically designed for case–control studies, which assesses the risk of bias in observational research. This scale consists of 8 items divided into three key components: the selection of cases and controls, the comparability of the groups, and the ascertainment of exposure. Each of these components was rated using the star system to provide a comprehensive assessment. Each study can receive a score between 0–9, and a score above 6 is considered acceptable [ 30 ]. All twelve studies received a score of 6 or higher and were thus included in the meta-analysis. Statistical analysis A meta-analysis was conducted to determine the pooled effect size of the standardized mean difference (Cohen's d ) of the GDNF between cases with SCZ and healthy controls. The studies were aggregated based on sample size, mean, and standard deviation of GDNF levels in both cases and controls. Pooled effect sizes for the between-group differences are presented along with 95% confidence intervals (95% CI) in a forest plot. Because all individual studies were from Asian and European regions, we also calculated pooled estimates for the geographic subgroups, the results of which were depicted by another forest plot. We analyzed several other subgroups as follows: age of onset of the disease (< 25 years vs. ≥ 25 years), the average length of the disease duration (< 10 years vs. ≥ 10 years), Chlorpromazine daily dose (< 500 mg vs. ≥ 500 mg), and the average total score of PANSS (scores < 80 vs. ≥ 80). We used several meta-regressions with the method of moments to assess the effect of mean age of samples, sex ratio, quality of the study, year of study, age of illness onset, disease duration, Chlorpromazine dose, and the PANSS scores on the pooled estimates. An I 2 of 50% and above was used to detect heterogeneity and, in this case, the random-effects method was used to compute all pooled estimates. However, we also reported the estimates for the fixed-effects method. Egger's statistic was employed to detect potential publication bias, which was depicted using a funnel plot. All hypotheses were tested at a significance level of p < 0.05, utilizing the Comprehensive Meta-Analysis (CMA.2) software. Results Study and sample characteristics This meta-analysis includes data from 1,510 participants, including 817 individuals diagnosed with SCZ and 691 healthy controls. The included studies were published between 2014 and 2023 and exhibited a range of sample sizes varying from 48 to 282 participants. The mean age of participants ranged from 24.4 ± 5.7 years to 52.85 ± 6.4 years. In many studies, the control group was paired with the case group based on gender and age. The antipsychotic dosage ranged from 100 to 748 mg of chlorpromazine equivalents per day. The characteristics and significant findings from the studies included in the analysis are outlined in Table 1 . The funnel plot (see Fig. 2 ) did not show any publication bias (Egger t value = 0.037, p = 0.971). Figure 3 shows the standardized mean difference in the GDNF between cases and controls. As can be seen, there is a significant difference between SCZ and healthy controls in both the random-effects ( d = –0.80, p < 0.001) and the fixed-effects ( d = –0.79, z = –14.031, p < 0.001) estimates. Fig. 2 Funnel plot for identifying publication bias Fig. 3 Forest plot for the standardized mean difference in the GDNF between cases and controls Meta-regression and subgroup analysis To find the source of heterogeneity in this study, Meta-regression analysis was conducted for age of onset, duration of the disease, Chlorpromazine dose, total PANSS score, age mean, sex ratio, year of study, and quality of study between the groups, showing an affected p -value for sex ratio and year of publication (< 0.05). Table 2 shows the details of the results of subgroup analysis and meta-regression analysis. When we estimated the standardized mean differences for the geographic subgroups (Asian vs. European samples), subgroup analyses indicated that the standardized mean difference of GDNF was larger in European samples. The random-effects estimates were –0.61 [CI: –1.13, –0.10; p = 0.019] and –1.01 [CI: –1.59, –0.43; p < 0.001] for the Asia and Europe regions, respectively. Other subgroups analyzed included age of disease onset. The results showed relatively equivalent levels of GDNF in both subgroups. The random-effects estimates were –0.77 [CI: –1.45, –0.09; p = 0.027] for age of onset < 25 years and –0.67 [CI: –1.25, –0.09; p = 0.024] for age of onset ≥ 25 years. When we estimated the standardized mean differences for the average duration of the disease (< 10 years vs. ≥ 10 years), the results showed a significant difference between the subgroups. The random-effects estimates were –0.93 [CI: –1.89, 0.03; p = 0.058] for the disease duration < 10 years while it was –0.82 [CI: –1.34, –0.30; p = 0.002] for the disease duration ≥ 10 years. In our subgroup analysis of subjects with SCZ, we found that GDNF levels were lower in non-medicated individuals compared to those who were medicated. The random-effects estimates were –1.08 [CI: –1.18, –0.22; p = 0.004] in non-medicated patients, while it was –0.73 [CI: –1.33, –0.82; p < 0.001] for medicated patients. A significant difference was shown between the subgroups with different doses of chlorpromazine. The random-effects estimates were –0.29 [CI: –1.01, 0.42; p = 0.420] for < 500 mg daily dose while it was –0.68 [CI: –1.15, –0.21; p = 0.005] for ≥ 500 mg daily dose. The subgroup analysis for the total score of PANSS showed relatively equivalent levels of GDNF in the subgroups. The random-effects estimates were –1.00 [CI: –1.51, –0.48; p < 0.001] for total PANSS < 80 and –0.96 [CI: –1.47, –0.44; p < 0.001] for total PANSS ≥ 80. Fig. 4 The results of sensitivity analysis Discussion This meta-analysis, which includes 12 studies with over 1,500 participants, examined the role of GDNF in SCZ. Previous research has established the role of GDNF in various mental disorders, including mood disorders [ 19 , 31 ], anxiety [ 20 ], and bipolar disorder [ 32 ]. Our analysis extends these findings to SCZ, confirming an association between lower levels of GDNF and the psychiatric condition. This represents the first comprehensive meta-analysis addressing this subject. The high heterogeneity across studies led us to use a random-effects method for pooled estimates. Since heterogeneity can arise from differences in study populations, interventions, outcomes, or methodologies, we estimated effect sizes across subgroups within studies. Additionally, meta-regression analysis was used to better understand the effects of several moderators on the pooled estimates. Our findings indicate that patients with SCZ exhibit significantly lower circulating GDNF levels compared to healthy controls. This reduction is particularly pronounced in untreated patients and appears to correlate with the dosage of antipsychotic medication. The majority of evidence supports a negative association between GDNF levels and SCZ, while some studies have reported conflicting results [ 25 – 27 ]. These discrepancies may arise from variations in sample size, patient demographics, and the complex functions of neurotrophic factors in psychiatric conditions. The meta-regression analysis suggests that combined estimates remain unaffected by variations in the average age of case and control groups, indicating that included studies likely employed age-matching techniques to reduce the impact of confounding variables. Notably, our analysis found higher GDNF levels in studies involving European samples, which may reflect differences in genetics, nutrition, and lifestyle among populations[ 33 – 35 ]. We did not find a relationship between the age of onset and GDNF levels, a finding supported by several studies [ 7 , 10 , 12 , 23 ]. This suggests that while GDNF has protective roles for neurons, it may not directly influence the onset of SCZ. Other unknown factors could contribute to disease onset, warranting further investigation. Additionally, we identified a significant correlation between GDNF levels and disease duration; specifically, longer disease duration is associated with lower GDNF values. This finding aligns with several studies [ 7 , 10 ] but contradicts others [ 23 , 26 ], potentially due to small sample size or methodological differences. Furthermore, our study found that GDNF levels were lower in non-medicated subjects compared to those receiving antipsychotic treatment. This highlights the potential impact of these medications on GDNF levels and suggests that antipsychotics may confer neuroprotective effects beyond symptom management by modulating neurotrophic factors. The relationship between daily antipsychotic dosage and GDNF levels further corroborates the notion that antipsychotics play a significant role not only in managing psychiatric symptoms but also in promoting neuroprotection through the modulation of neurotrophic factors [ 7 ]. Given the observed associations between GDNF levels and cognitive function, there is potential for GDNF to serve as a bioecological marker for both diagnosis and treatment response in SCZ. As a biomarker, GDNF could provide insights into disease progression and therapeutic efficacy. For instance, lower serum GDNF levels might indicate a more severe illness state or poorer treatment responses [ 7 ]. Conversely, increases in GDNF levels following antipsychotic treatment could reflect neuroprotective effects and improvements in cognitive function [ 27 ]. Therefore, monitoring GDNF levels could enhance personalized treatment approaches for individuals with SCZ. A study involving mice with a heterozygous GDNF mutation indicated impaired cognitive performance in water-maze tasks [ 36 ], underscoring GDNF's role in cognitive function. Additionally, reductions in psychiatric symptoms during antipsychotic treatment was linked to a gradual increase in GDNF levels [ 7 ], proposing that GDNF may play a role in both the etiology and pharmacotherapy of SCZ. Despite our findings supporting a significant association between GDNF levels and SCZ, the relationship between GDNF levels and specific symptom domains remains complex. Our analysis did not identify a direct correlation with total PANSS scores, consistent with findings from two studies [ 8 , 10 ]. This suggests that while GDNF may influence certain aspects of SCZ, it does not directly correlate with all symptom dimensions assessed by the PANSS. However, some studies have reported correlations between GDNF levels and negative subscales of PANSS [ 12 , 23 ], indicating a nuanced relationship influenced by variables such as race, treatment type and dosage, and patient age. Limitations and future directions Several limitations should be considered when interpreting our findings. First, the extent to which GDNF can cross the blood–brain barrier remains unclear, limiting our ability to directly link peripheral GDNF levels to central nervous system processes. Second, the limited number of studies and the heterogeneity of patient populations may have influenced the observed effects. Third, most research is cross-sectional, limiting insights into how GDNF levels change over time in relation to treatment response. Importantly, potential publication bias must also be acknowledged as a limitation. The tendency for studies with positive results to be published more frequently than those with negative or inconclusive findings can skew our understanding of the true relationship between GDNF levels and SCZ. Future research should aim for comprehensive reporting practices that include all results—regardless of outcome—to provide a more accurate picture of this relationship. Future research should focus on clarifying the precise mechanisms linking GDNF to SCZ, investigating potential therapeutic implications of GDNF modulation, and exploring its role as a biomarker for disease progression and treatment response. Additionally, examining relationships between GDNF and other biomarkers, such as inflammatory markers and neuroimaging findings, may provide further insights into SCZ's pathophysiology. Conclusion This systematic review and meta-analysis underscore the significant association between lower levels of GDNF and SCZ, emphasizing its potential role as a biomarker for this disorder. Our findings suggest that GDNF may not only contribute to SCZ's pathophysiology but also serve as a target for therapeutic intervention, particularly within the context of antipsychotic treatment. While further investigation is warranted regarding the relationship between GDNF levels and various clinical factors such as medication dosage and disease duration, our results advocate for more extensive research into the neuroprotective properties of GDNF. Understanding these dynamics could pave the way for novel treatment strategies aimed at enhancing cognitive function and improving overall patient outcomes in SCZ. documents.title: Predictors of long-term outcome of patients with schizophrenia in Africa: systematic review and meta-analysis.
documents.abstract:
BACKGROUND: One of the most compelling areas of schizophrenia research involves the investigation of its longitudinal course and clinical outcomes. Longitudinal studies have provided profound insights into the trajectory of schizophrenia, elucidating its progression, clinical phenotype, functional impairments, treatment responsiveness, and key prognostic determinants. While contemporary therapeutic interventions have demonstrated promise in altering disease trajectory and enhancing recovery, schizophrenia remains characterized by heterogeneous outcomes, distinguishing it from other psychotic disorders. This review aims to assess the pooled prevalence of positive outcomes and identify key predictors on individuals with schizophrenia disorder across Africa.
METHODS: A comprehensive systematic search was conducted across multiple databases, including PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, African Journal Online, PsycINFO, EMBASE, Psychiatry Online, CINAHL, Science Direct, and the Cochrane Library. This review includes observational studies, comprising both cross-sectional and cohort designs, published between 1993 and 2024, that evaluate the prognosis and favorable clinical outcomes of schizophrenia in Africa. The literature search was performed between November 2, 2024, and December 20, 2024. A total of sixteen original research articles assessing the prevalence of favorable outcomes in individuals with schizophrenia met the inclusion criteria. Data extraction was conducted independently by two reviewers to ensure methodological rigor, and the review is registered with PROSPERO (ID: CRD42024613692).
RESULTS: The pooled prevalence of positive outcomes among individuals with schizophrenia disorder in Africa was estimated at 44.17% (95% CI: 32.27-56.08). Among a total of 2,263 individuals, the aggregated remission rate across 13 studies was 48.14%, while the pooled recovery rate was 42% among 474 individuals across 4 studies. Furthermore, significant predictors of positive outcomes included the presence of prominent positive symptoms (OR = 1.89, 95% CI: 1.24-2.89), prolonged antipsychotic use (OR = 2.15, 95% CI: 1.69-2.74), and good medication adherence (OR = 4.31, 95% CI: 2.17-8.56).
CONCLUSION: This review reveals that nearly half of individuals with schizophrenia in Africa achieve favorable outcomes, despite ongoing challenges. Key predictors-prominent positive symptoms, prolonged antipsychotic use, and good medication adherence-significantly influence prognosis. These findings underscore the need for early, personalized interventions and sustained treatment adherence. Given the heterogeneity of outcomes, region-specific strategies are essential to optimize care.

Keywords Long-term Outcome Schizophrenia Meta-analysis Africa pmc-status-qastatus 0 pmc-status-live yes pmc-status-embargo no pmc-status-released yes pmc-prop-open-access yes pmc-prop-olf no pmc-prop-manuscript no pmc-prop-legally-suppressed no pmc-prop-has-pdf yes pmc-prop-has-supplement yes pmc-prop-pdf-only no pmc-prop-suppress-copyright no pmc-prop-is-real-version no pmc-prop-is-scanned-article no pmc-prop-preprint no pmc-prop-in-epmc yes pmc-license-ref CC BY-NC-ND issue-copyright-statement © BioMed Central Ltd., part of Springer Nature 2025 Introduction Schizophrenia is a persistent mental illness marked by delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, and poor cognitive function [ 1 , 2 ]. Longitudinal research on schizophrenia has changed the outlook on its nature, providing more detailed information on its course, positive outcome, diagnostic issues, symptoms, functioning problems, treatment, and prognostic factors [ 3 – 5 ]. One of the most fascinating aspects of schizophrenia research is the study of its course and outcome [ 6 ]. Outcome is a multidimensional construct made up of two components: course, which refers to the pattern of sickness progression, and outcome, which is the individual’s status at a certain moment in time [ 7 , 8 ]. Outcome is a multidimensional construct that includes clinical symptoms, social functioning, work performance, cognitive function, family load, and quality of life as influenced by schizophrenia course [ 9 ]. Historically, research on the clinical course and outcomes of schizophrenia has predominantly focused on positive psychotic symptoms; however, contemporary treatment paradigms now prioritize achieving comprehensive functional recovery and clinically meaningful outcomes for patients, caregivers, and clinicians [ 10 – 12 ]. The consensus definition of symptomatic remission has recently emphasized the need to expand outcome assessments in psychosis to include negative symptoms, which are strongly associated with functional outcomes [ 13 , 14 ]. Remission is considered a critical prerequisite for full recovery [ 15 ]. Moreover, emerging evidence suggests that early interventions targeting functional and vocational recovery may mitigate or even eliminate long-term psychotic symptoms and associated disability, highlighting the reciprocal relationship between symptomatic and functional recovery [ 16 , 17 ]. While the concept of symptomatic remission is well-defined, definitions of functional remission and recovery remain contentious [ 18 ]. The notion of recovery holds significant implications for fostering hope among individuals with schizophrenia, their families, and mental health professionals [ 19 , 20 ]. Unlike remission, which is more precisely defined, recovery encompasses broader, more abstract dimensions, such as productivity, functional independence, the ability to maintain fulfilling relationships, empowerment, and the overcoming of internalized stigma and multifaceted process, in which alleviation of psychotic symptoms represents only one component of the broader journey toward recovery [ 21 – 23 ]. According to recent studies, contemporary treatment strategies may result in a moderate improvement in illness course and complete recovery for some schizophrenic patients [ 7 , 24 ]. However, longitudinal research from the Chicago Follow-up Study and the World Health Organization Study shows that, despite modern treatment, schizophrenia patients have a worse course and outcome than other psychotic and nonpsychotic patients, with more recurrent psychopathology during the early stages [ 5 , 25 , 26 ]. The study utilized symptomatology and psychosocial data to predict outcomes after a 15-year follow-up in 92 individuals diagnosed with schizophrenia: The discriminant analytical technique accounted for 23% of the variance in outcomes, a notable reduction compared to the 49% variance explained in a previous study [ 27 ]. A meta-analysis examining studies with a minimum follow-up period of one year revealed that 40.2% of patients exhibited a positive outcome after an average follow-up of 5.6 years [ 28 ]. However, in approximately 50% of schizophrenia patients, there is a significant lack of awareness regarding their mental condition, its symptoms, and associated implications. Furthermore, diminished insight into the disorder is strongly correlated with poorer long-term outcomes [ 29 , 30 ]. In recent decades, there has been an increasing interest in recovery and remission in schizophrenia, which has inspired efforts to define recovery as a combination of clinical and social remission, with either clinical or social remission lasting at least two years [ 14 , 31 , 32 ]. While mortality rate is often neglected in outcome studies, but recently, substantial mortality rates have been reported from low- and middle-income countries in schizophrenia outcome studies [ 33 , 34 ]. First-episode schizophrenia patients have a higher mortality rate due to unnatural causes and lifestyle factors such as smoking, inactivity, and antipsychotics; this widening mortality difference may not reflect deteriorating conditions, but rather under-improvement in comparison to the general population [ 35 – 37 ]. In developing nations, schizophrenia patients live with their partners and communicate their thoughts and feelings; this mental support allows them to live a normal life and influences their outcome [ 38 ]. Researchers discovered markers of symptomatic remission, including greater premorbid adjustment, functioning, lower psychopathology, shorter period of untreated psychosis, and early recovery following treatment [ 39 , 40 ]. But patients who have medication non-adherence, substance use disorder, and a high emotional home environment all have a significant impact on relapse rates, with prior hospitalization being a major predictor of future hospitalization [ 41 , 42 ]. Stabilization and control of symptoms are critical for preventing psychotic relapse, which can predict the prognosis within the first five years of beginning [ 43 ]. In personal recovery, there was a slight to moderate negative connection between symptom severity and functional recovery, indicating that each outcome should have its own predictors [ 44 ]. Although primary studies on the prognosis and positive outcomes of schizophrenia in African populations remain limited, existing reports exhibit substantial variability and notable inconsistency in their findings. Furthermore, to our knowledge, no prior systematic reviews or meta-analyses have comprehensively synthesized the pooled prevalence and determinants of favorable outcomes in individuals with schizophrenia in Africa. This review seeks to systematically evaluate the pooled prevalence of positive clinical outcomes and identify key prognostic factors in individuals with schizophrenia within the African context. Methods Search strategy and selection criteria The protocol for the current systematic review and meta-analysis was registered in the International Prospective Register of Systemic Review (PROSPERO) (ID = CRD42024613692). We used an appropriate guideline for systematic reviews and meta-analyses reports, which is the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA-2020) [ 45 ]. We conducted a comprehensive search of primary articles in multiple databases, including PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, African Journal Online, EMBASE, Psychiatry Online, CINAHL, Science Direct, and the Cochrane Library. The search was conducted from November 2, 2024, to December 20, 2024, for articles published between 1993 and 2024. Using relevant MeSH (Medical Subject Headings) terms, the electronic search was structured with the following keywords: (outcome OR prognosis OR remission OR recovery OR improvement) AND (prevalence OR magnitude OR epidemiology OR correlation) AND (schizophrenia OR schizophrenia spectrum disorders OR psychotic disorder OR severe mental illness) AND (factor OR risk OR predictors OR determinant) AND (Southern Africa OR Central Africa OR East Africa OR North Africa OR Western Africa OR Sub-Saharan Africa OR Africa). Additionally, reference lists of the identified articles were manually reviewed, including publications from the World Psychiatric Association and the African Association of Psychiatrists and Allied Professions, to identify further relevant studies. The inclusion criteria for this systematic review and meta-analysis were as follows: (1) observational studies, including cross-sectional and cohort designs, that evaluated the prevalence and associated factors of outcomes in patients diagnosed with schizophrenia, with participants aged 18 years and older, conducted in Africa; (2) original studies with complete and readily accessible data; (3) studies published in the English language. Exclusion criteria were: (I) studies that did not report the outcome variables; (II) studies with incomplete or inaccessible data; (III) studies with potentially biased prevalence estimates, such as those involving substance-induced psychosis, refractory schizophrenia, schizophrenia-like psychosis due to epilepsy, or homelessness; (IV) case reports, reviews, case studies, conference abstracts, qualitative studies, and short communications; and (V) studies with samples not representative of the broader schizophrenia population, including those focused on specific subgroups based on gender, age, or racial categories. Data extraction The two investigators (MK and GK) independently conducted data extraction and quality assessment using detailed information forms. They utilized a standardized data extraction format developed in Microsoft Excel to systematically extract relevant data after thoroughly reviewing the titles, abstracts, and full texts of the studies, ensuring the article’s originality. Disagreements regarding study eligibility were resolved through discussion; with intervention by a third author (SF) when necessary. The final data extraction format included the publication year, the first author’s name, the type of diagnosis, the countries where the study was conducted, the institution’s location, sample size, study design, tools used to assess improvement scales, and the prevalence of outcomes. The second objective was to extract relevant variables, including the odds ratio and 95% confidence intervals, associated with remission or clinical outcomes. The quality of the primary studies included in this systematic review and meta-analysis was assessed using the modified Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) Critical Appraisal Checklist for Prevalence Studies to evaluate the risk of bias [ 45 , 46 ]. Studies with a JBI score exceeding 5 were included for data synthesis. Additionally, the quality of two articles was assessed using the 9-star Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS). For case-control studies, the evaluation focused on the selection, comparability, and exposure criteria, while for cohort studies, the assessment addressed selection, comparability, and outcome measure [ 47 , 48 ]. Only studies with a NOS score greater than 5 were included for data synthesis. Risk of bias (quality) assessment To assess the risk of bias in observational studies, we employed the modified Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) Critical Appraisal Checklist and the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS). The quality of the included studies was evaluated using these tools, which are widely recognized and frequently utilized in systematic reviews and meta-analyses within this field [ 49 – 52 ](Tables 1 and 2 ). Outcome measurements This review was guided by two primary objectives. The first objective was to determine the pooled prevalence of positive outcomes among African individuals diagnosed with schizophrenia. The Composite International Diagnostic Interview (CIDI), as well as the subsequent Determinants of Outcomes of Severe Mental Disorder (DOSMD) tools, was referenced to evaluate the differential course of schizophrenia, with evidence suggesting more favorable outcomes in emerging nations compared to developed countries. To assess symptom severity and treatment response, the Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale (PANSS) was utilized, while the Brief Psychiatric Rating Scale (BPRS) was employed to measure psychiatric symptoms in psychotic disorders. Additionally, the Global Assessment of Functioning (GAF) scale was used to assess the degree of impairment in daily functioning, with a range from 0 to 100, indicating the severity of functional interference due to the disorder. The second objective of this review was to estimate the pooled effect size of relevant determinants influencing outcomes among adult schizophrenia patients in Africa. STATA version 14.0 was employed to compute the pooled prevalence of positive outcomes, and the odds ratio was utilized to quantify the combined effect size of various determinants on clinical outcomes. The odds ratio was derived using two-by-two tables from the findings reported in the primary studies included in the review. Data analysis The data extracted from the Microsoft Excel spreadsheet were subsequently imported into STATA 14.0 for comprehensive statistical analysis. A random-effects meta-analysis was conducted to estimate the pooled effect size across all studies, with a 95% confidence interval. The findings from this systematic review and meta-analysis are presented in textual summaries, accompanied by forest plots and tabular representations. Descriptive statistics, including means, standard deviations, medians, and means, were employed to summarize prevalence estimates and other continuous variables. Statistical heterogeneity was evaluated using the I² statistic, and in light of the observed variability across studies, a random-effects model was applied for the meta-analysis [ 53 , 54 ]. Subgroup analysis was conducted using publication year, types of medication, type of study design, type of tools used to assess the improvement and country, and the presence of any possible source of heterogeneity was checked using sensitivity analysis. Publication bias of the included studies was assessed by using both visual observation of the symmetry in the funnel plots, and Egger weighted regression tests at a 5% significant level [ 55 – 57 ]. In Egger’s test, publication bias was considered to occur when the p-value was less than 0.05. Results Search results A total of 1,065 studies were identified through a comprehensive electronic search across multiple databases, including PubMed, Google Scholar, CINHAL, and African Journal Online, The search was conducted from November 2, 2024, to December 20, 2024, for articles published between 1993 and 2024. After removing 79 duplicate records, 980 studies remained for screening. Title and abstract screening led to the exclusion of 913 studies due to reasons such as lack of relevance to the research question, non-African study settings, unavailability of full texts, or incompatible study populations. Full-text assessments were conducted for 73 articles, of which 57 were excluded based on predefined eligibility criteria. Ultimately, 16 studies met the inclusion criteria and were included in this systematic review and meta-analysis (Fig. 1 ). Fig. 1 PRISMA flow chart of study selection meta- analysis of long-term outcomes among individual with schizophrenia disorder in Africa Characteristics of the included studies This systematic review and meta-analysis incorporates sixteen primary studies examining positive outcomes and key determinants in individuals with schizophrenia in Africa. Among these, eight studies utilized a cross-sectional design to assess prevalence or effect size, two employed a retrospective cohort design, and six adopted a prospective cohort design. These studies were systematically included to provide a comprehensive analysis of the relevant outcomes and determinants in this population. The research covered five African countries: four studies in Ethiopia [ 58 – 61 ], three studies in Egypt [ 62 – 64 ], four in Tunisia [ 65 – 68 ], four studies in Nigeria [ 69 – 72 ], and one study in South Africa [ 73 ]. This observational study design, which was used in all of the key studies in this review, included 2,665 participants. Studies found that the prevalence of outcome among schizophrenia patients was highest in Nigeria (85.8%) and lowest in Ethiopia (20%). Regarding assessment tools, seven articles used the Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale (PANSS), three used the Brief Psychiatric Rating Scale (BPRS), one used the Global Assessment of Functioning (GAF), two used the Composite International Diagnostic Interview (CIDI), one article used the Determinants of Outcomes of Severe Mental Disorder (DOSMD), one used Global Functioning: Social (GF: Social), and one used the Recovery Assessment Scale (RAS). Regarding the types of prescribed antipsychotic medications, it was observed that 12 studies included participants who were concurrently receiving both first- and second-generation antipsychotics; three studies were prescribed risperidone and olanzapine as the main antipsychotic treatments, while one study specifically investigated the use of clozapine (Table 1 ). The pooled prevalence of positive outcomes was 44.17% (95% CI: 32.27–56.08). Among a total of 2,263 individuals, the pooled remission rate was 48.14% based on data from 13 studies. Additionally, the pooled recovery rate was 42%, derived from 474 individuals across four studies (Fig. 2 ). Fig. 2 Forest plot illustrating the effect sizes (ES) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) from multiple studies assessing positive outcomes in individuals with schizophrenia in African populations. Each study is listed on the left, with corresponding effect size estimates and confidence intervals presented on the right. The size of each square reflects the study’s relative weight in the meta-analysis, determined using a random effects model. The overall pooled estimate of positive outcomes is represented by a diamond at the bottom, yielding a summary effect size of 44.17% (32.27, 56.08). The substantial heterogeneity observed (I² = 97.9%, p < 0.001) indicates significant variability among the included studies Heterogeneity and publication bias The random-effects model considers both intra- and inter-participant variability (heterogeneity). The majority of random effect pooled rate prevalence of outcome values were high (I2 = 97.9%), indicating a high level of heterogeneity. High heterogeneity and the lack of statistical significance in some subgroup analyses suggest that results should be treated with caution. Regarding publication bias, two techniques were used to check if there was a publication bias in the included studies. The first was checked by a funnel plot, which showed the symmetric distribution and revealed the absence of publication bias in the included articles (Fig. 3 ). Additionally, the Eggers test was used to confirm that there was no publication bias, as shown by P = 0.436 (Table 2 ). Fig. 3 Funnel plot assessing publication bias with pseudo 95% confidence limits. Each dot represents an individual study. The vertical line indicates the summary effect size, and the dashed lines represent the 95% confidence limits. As the results show, all of the values fall within the expected 95% CI, providing that the exclusion of a single study did not significantly alter the prevalence of this review (Fig. 4 ). Fig. 4 Sensitivity analysis of long-term outcomes among individuals with schizophrenia disorder in Africa Subgroup analysis The pooled prevalence of favorable outcomes exhibited significant heterogeneity; therefore, a subgroup analysis was conducted based on factors such as study country, publication year, types of screening tools, and the various study designs employed to measure outcomes. The subgroup analysis revealed notable variability in the pooled prevalence of positive outcomes among schizophrenia patients with favorable prognosis across different countries. In Nigeria, the prevalence was 62.43% (95% CI: 41.96–82.89), followed by Egypt at 45.01% (95% CI: 17.68–72.34), Tunisia at 39.61% (95% CI: 20.74–58.49), Ethiopia at 33.69% (95% CI: 20.57–46.82), and South Africa, which exhibited the lowest improvement of 20.9% (95% CI: 20.02–37.98). Regarding study design, cross-sectional studies showed a higher pooled prevalence of positive outcomes (55.7%, 95% CI: 41.28–70.12), followed by retrospective cohort studies (39.79%, 95% CI: 14.89–64.69), and prospective cohort studies, which reported the lowest prevalence (30.54%, 95% CI: 23.12–37.96). Additionally, studies conducted after 2019 demonstrated a higher pooled prevalence of favorable outcomes (51%, 95% CI: 35.16–66.83), compared to studies conducted prior to 2019 (37.56%, 95% CI: 25.68–49.44). The RAS screening tool was associated with the highest prevalence of positive outcomes (69.5%, 95% CI: 63.12–75.88), followed by the BPRS (52.8%, 95% CI: 17.56–88.04), PANSS (46.43%, 95% CI: 35.26–57.59), and DOSMD (38.85%, 95% CI: 16.02–61.68). The Composite International Diagnostic Interview (CIDI) showed the lowest prevalence of positive outcomes at 20% (95% CI: 15.62–24.38). In terms of treatment response, patients treated with both typical and atypical antipsychotics exhibited a response rate of 46.81% (95% CI: 31.94–61.66), followed by those treated with risperidone and olanzapine (39.02%, 95% CI: 22.56–55.47), while the lowest response rate was observed in patients receiving clozapine (27%, 95% CI: 3.78–46.21) (Table 3 ). Patients exhibiting prominent positive psychotic symptoms were found to have 1.89 times higher odds of achieving good outcomes compared to those with negative or other psychotic symptoms (OR = 1.89, 95% CI: 1.24–2.89). Furthermore, individuals with good adherence to antipsychotic medication were 4.31 times more likely to attain good outcomes than those with poor adherence (OR = 4.31, 95% CI: 2.17–8.56). Additionally, patients who received antipsychotic treatment for an adequate duration had 2.15 times higher odds of positive outcomes compared to those who did not comply with the recommended treatment duration (OR = 2.15, 95% CI: 1.69–2.74) (Fig. 5 ). Fig. 5 Meta-analysis of data from well-documented studies assessing positive indicators of schizophrenia disorders in African populations. Each square represents the estimated odds ratio (OR) from an individual study, with horizontal lines indicating the corresponding 95% confidence intervals (CI). The size of each square is proportional to the study’s weight in the meta-analysis. An odds ratio higher suggests a strong predictive value for schizophrenia-related outcomes. The diamonds represent the pooled effect estimates, with their width reflecting the 95% CI. A random-effects model was used to account for variability among studies Discussion This review included a total of 2,665 participants to evaluate the pooled prevalence and associated determinants of positive outcomes in individuals with schizophrenia across Africa. Our primary conclusion highlights the variability in outcome assessment techniques, with the most substantial improvements observed in the Recovery Assessment Scale (RAS), Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale (PANSS), and Brief Psychiatric Rating Scale (BPRS), while minimal changes were detected using the Composite International Diagnostic Interview (CIDI) evaluation tool. The methodologies employed in this study were designed to quantify variability within individual nations while ensuring a standardized approach across datasets. However, these algorithms inherently assume uniform data quality and may not fully capture the cultural, linguistic, or contextual nuances present in the original sources. To mitigate these limitations, we conducted within-nation analyses to minimize cross-national confounding and applied consistent methodological approaches across all datasets. Additionally, we performed sensitivity analyses to confirm the robustness of our findings across different computational techniques. Despite legitimate concerns about the pooled prevalence of long-term outcomes and the well-appreciated heterogeneity in the estimates, we identified pooled prevalence for long-term outcomes [ 74 – 76 ]. While this meta-analysis study aims to narrow the data gap in this area by complementing strong evidence on the prevalence of symptoms remission and its associated variables in individuals with schizophrenia, it was based on obtaining an average estimate of the prevalence of favorable outcomes in Africa, which was 44.17% with a 95% CI (32.27–56.08), which aligns with similar studies conducted in Germany 48% [ 77 ], in Japan 46% [ 78 ], in Singapore 38.4% [ 79 ], in Indonesia 43.5% [ 80 ]. The pooled prevalence of positive outcomes was lower than other studies that were conducted in different countries in systematic and meta-analysis done in India 72.3% [ 81 ], in UK 58% [ 82 ], in China 57.3% [ 83 ], in France 60.6% [ 84 ], According to a meta-analysis conducted in Asian countries, approximately 60% of people with schizophrenia demonstrate significant clinical improvement, while a slightly smaller percentage show functional improvement [ 85 ]. The possible reason for the discrepancy might be the difference in cultural and socioeconomic factors. Variations in healthcare systems, such as access to psychiatric treatment, medication availability, and rehabilitation service integration, play an important role. Countries with greater mental health care infrastructure are more likely to achieve positive outcomes. Cultural attitudes about mental health, access to community assistance, and stigma may all have an impact on long-term outcomes [ 86 – 88 ]. Another justification may be the most recent antipsychotics, which are frequently favored due to their lower risk of extrapyramidal side effects, are more expensive and may not be generally accessible. Patients in developing countries may rely on older, first-generation antipsychotics, which can lead to lower adherence due to side effects. Additionally, frequent shortages of essential medications, inconsistent supply chains, and a lack of local pharmaceutical production all contribute to treatment gaps [ 89 , 90 ]. The pooled prevalence of favorable outcomes was higher than other studies that were conducted in different countries in meta-analysis done on early onset schizophrenia in Denmark 15.4% [ 91 ], in Brazil 23% [ 92 ], in India 30.5% [ 93 ], in Canada 18% [ 94 ], another study in Denmark 24.2% [ 31 ], in USA 25% [ 95 ], meta-analysis done in Finland 13.5% [ 32 ]. The reason may be the overall prevalence of positive outcomes in early-onset schizophrenia varies by country due to variances in healthcare systems, cultural factors, diagnostic criteria, treatment availability, and follow-up procedures [ 96 , 97 ]. Certainly! The observation that schizophrenia patients in developing countries might exhibit better outcomes than those in Western countries is an interesting paradox and has been noted in several studies. However, the findings from your systematic review and meta-analysis did not show a clear pattern of superior outcomes in African nations compared to Western nations. Here’s a deeper look at possible reasons for this discrepancy: In many African societies, the prominence of community and familial networks plays a crucial role in the management of chronic conditions such as schizophrenia. These strong social structures often provide patients with direct, ongoing support, which may enhance treatment adherence and improve overall outcomes, despite limitations in formal healthcare infrastructure. This contrasts with the situation in many Western countries, where individuals with schizophrenia frequently face greater social isolation, exacerbated by stigma, and may have less engagement with cohesive support systems, potentially contributing to poorer long-term outcomes [ 98 – 100 ]. This review revealed that favorable outcomes in patients with positive symptoms increased by 1.89 times higher odds of good outcomes compared to patients with negative and other types of psychotic symptoms. This finding was in supported with the study conducted in Japan [ 101 ], in India [ 102 ] and in Germany [ 103 ]. A possible justification for this may be Positive symptoms are more receptive to antipsychotic drugs, which are often more effective at treating hallucinations and delusions Negative symptoms, including apathy and social disengagement, are often chronic and exhibit limited responsiveness not only to conventional pharmacological treatments but also to psychological interventions, such as Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for psychosis (CBTp), particularly in individuals with treatment-resistant schizophrenia [ 104 ]. Furthermore, positive symptoms’ underlying neurobiological mechanisms may allow for earlier stabilization with proper therapy, whereas negative symptoms may include structural or functional brain alterations that are more difficult to reverse [ 105 – 107 ]. Furthermore, individuals with good adherence to antipsychotic medication were 4.31 times more likely to attain favorable outcomes than those with poor medication adherence. This finding was in supported with the study conducted in USA [ 108 ]. A possible justification may be to sustain a consistent therapeutic effect; antipsychotics must be used on a regular basis, which aids in the control of core symptoms such as hallucinations, delusions, and mood instability. Adherent patients are more likely to have consistent symptom reduction. Noncompliance might result in abrupt discontinuance or inconsistent dose, which increases the risk of symptom worsening or recurrence. Antipsychotics function by regulating neurotransmitters such as dopamine and serotonin. Adherence ensures that these metabolic processes are constantly regulated, which aids in achieving remission. Irregular use of antipsychotics can result in tolerance, resistance, or withdrawal symptoms, reducing the treatment’s effectiveness. So adherence helps to reduce these risks [ 109 – 111 ]. Additionally, patients who received antipsychotic treatment for an adequate duration had 2.15 times higher odds of positive outcomes compared to those who did not comply with the recommended treatment duration This finding was in supported with the study conducted in European countries [ 112 ], in Brazil [ 113 ]. in USA [ 5 ] and systematic review and meta-analysis done in Finland [ 25 ]. The reason may be antipsychotics require time to achieve their full therapeutic potential. An adequate duration allows the medication to stabilize neurotransmitter imbalances effectively, resulting in symptom improvement. Prolonged treatment can help in normalizing the over-activity or under-activity in brain circuits associated with psychosis, which is essential for achieving remission. Stopping medication prematurely can lead to a rebound in symptoms or relapse. Patients adhering to the treatment for the recommended duration are less likely to experience these issues [ 114 – 116 ]. The paradox of more favorable outcomes in low-resource settings, such as those observed in some African contexts, requires deeper examination, as it likely arises from a complex interplay of sociocultural, economic, and healthcare system factors. While developed countries generally benefit from advanced healthcare infrastructure, access to newer pharmacological treatments, and more comprehensive mental health care systems, outcomes in Africa may be influenced by unique social and cultural factors, including strong community and familial support networks, which mitigate the challenges posed by limited access to formal psychiatric care. These factors may play a critical role in shaping the prognosis for individuals with schizophrenia, despite the constraints of healthcare infrastructure. However, the discrepancies in outcomes across different regions necessitate further scientific investigation to better understand how cultural attitudes, the availability and type of treatment, and the broader healthcare context influence long-term clinical and functional recovery in schizophrenia patients. Future studies should aim to delineate the mechanisms by which these factors interact, in order to develop context-specific, evidence-based interventions that can optimize schizophrenia care globally. Limitation This systematic review and meta-analysis offer several strengths; however, there are notable limitations in the combined effect of positive outcomes among individuals with schizophrenia. One limitation is that the review exclusively included studies published in English, potentially leading to less robust or less accurate estimates of schizophrenia outcomes. The meta-analysis incorporates studies published across different time periods, and advancements in schizophrenia treatment over time may affect the comparability of outcomes, with older studies possibly underestimating the effectiveness of newer therapeutic interventions. Additionally, the included research may not have adequately represented all regions of Africa, leading to potential underrepresentation of specific areas or populations, which could affect the generalizability of findings across the continent’s diverse healthcare systems, cultural practices, and socioeconomic conditions. Another limitation is the lack of uniformity in the definition of “outcome” across studies, such as clinical remission, positive outcomes, recovery, or overall prognosis, complicating the comparison and synthesis of results. Finally, substantial heterogeneity was observed in both the overall meta-analysis and subgroup analyses, and the review was based on a relatively small number of studies. Conclusion This review demonstrates that nearly half of individuals with schizophrenia in Africa experience favorable positive outcomes, though significant challenges remain. The identified predictors—prominent positive symptoms, prolonged antipsychotic use, and good medication adherence—highlight critical factors influencing prognosis. These findings emphasize the need for early, personalized interventions and continuous treatment adherence to improve outcomes. Given the diversity of positive outcomes observed, tailored strategies that account for regional and individual variations are essential for optimizing care. Future longitudinal studies are crucial to further explore the mechanisms underlying these outcomes and to develop targeted therapeutic approaches to enhance the improvement for individuals with schizophrenia in Africa. Additional studies focusing on the biological, social, and economic factors influencing positive outcomes in diverse African populations can provide deeper insights and inform policy. documents.title: Psychotropic medication non-adherence and its determinants among people living with mental illnesses in Ethiopia: systematic review and meta-analysis study.
documents.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Over half of patients take medications incorrectly, with non-adherence being a significant challenge in managing mental illnesses and to healthcare systems globally. In mental health, non-adherence to psychotropic medications exacerbates symptoms, increases relapse rates, and contributes to treatment resistance, higher hospitalization rates, and mortality. It also places a financial burden on healthcare systems through preventable hospitalizations and prolonged treatments. Understanding the prevalence and determinants of non-adherence is particularly critical in low-resource settings like Ethiopia, where mental health services are underfunded and sociocultural factors influence treatment behaviors. Therefore, this study aimed to estimate the pooled prevalence and determinants of psychotropic medication non-adherence in Ethiopia.
METHODS: Primary articles were sourced from PubMed (Medline), EMBASE, CINAHL, Web of Science, PsycINFO, Google, and Google Scholar. The review included studies reporting the prevalence and determinants of psychotropic medication non-adherence among individuals with mental illness. Data were extracted using Microsoft Excel and analyzed in STATA 14. A random effects model was applied to estimate the pooled prevalence, and subgroup analyses were performed to explore heterogeneity. Publication bias was assessed using Egger's test and a funnel plot.
RESULTS: Seventeen studies with 7,097 participants were included. The pooled prevalence of psychotropic medication non-adherence was 43.98% (38.15, 49.81). Subgroup analysis revealed regional variations with prevalence rates of 52.85% in Harari, 52.4% in Amhara, 46.39% in Oromia, 39.8% in Addis Ababa, and 27.42% in Tigray. Significant determinants included negative attitudes toward treatment (OR: 3.69; 95% CI: 2.73-4.99), lack of insight (OR: 3.20; 95% CI: 1.71-5.99), medication side effects (OR: 2.84; 95% CI: 2.05-3.93), perceived stigma (OR: 2.41; 95% CI: 1.87-3.10), substance use (OR: 2.36; 95% CI: 2.02-2.74), and poor social support (OR: 2.30; 95% CI: 1.61-3.29).
CONCLUSIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS: This study found that over four in ten people with mental illness were non-adherent to medications. It is recommended to design intervention strategies that address the factors associated with non-adherence to psychotropic medication.
PROSPERO REGISTRATION: CRD42024563343.

Background Over half of patients take medications incorrectly, with non-adherence being a significant challenge in managing mental illnesses and to healthcare systems globally. In mental health, non-adherence to psychotropic medications exacerbates symptoms, increases relapse rates, and contributes to treatment resistance, higher hospitalization rates, and mortality. It also places a financial burden on healthcare systems through preventable hospitalizations and prolonged treatments. Understanding the prevalence and determinants of non-adherence is particularly critical in low-resource settings like Ethiopia, where mental health services are underfunded and sociocultural factors influence treatment behaviors. Therefore, this study aimed to estimate the pooled prevalence and determinants of psychotropic medication non-adherence in Ethiopia. Methods Primary articles were sourced from PubMed (Medline), EMBASE, CINAHL, Web of Science, PsycINFO, Google, and Google Scholar. The review included studies reporting the prevalence and determinants of psychotropic medication non-adherence among individuals with mental illness. Data were extracted using Microsoft Excel and analyzed in STATA 14. A random effects model was applied to estimate the pooled prevalence, and subgroup analyses were performed to explore heterogeneity. Publication bias was assessed using Egger’s test and a funnel plot. Results Seventeen studies with 7,097 participants were included. The pooled prevalence of psychotropic medication non-adherence was 43.98% (38.15, 49.81). Subgroup analysis revealed regional variations with prevalence rates of 52.85% in Harari, 52.4% in Amhara, 46.39% in Oromia, 39.8% in Addis Ababa, and 27.42% in Tigray. Significant determinants included negative attitudes toward treatment (OR: 3.69; 95% CI: 2.73–4.99), lack of insight (OR: 3.20; 95% CI: 1.71–5.99), medication side effects (OR: 2.84; 95% CI: 2.05–3.93), perceived stigma (OR: 2.41; 95% CI: 1.87–3.10), substance use (OR: 2.36; 95% CI: 2.02–2.74), and poor social support (OR: 2.30; 95% CI: 1.61–3.29). Conclusions and recommendations This study found that over four in ten people with mental illness were non-adherent to medications. It is recommended to design intervention strategies that address the factors associated with non-adherence to psychotropic medication. Prospero registration CRD42024563343. According to the World Health Organization’s (WHO) 2022 report, one in eight people —970 million individuals —suffers from a mental illness, with prevalence varying by age and sex. Mental disorders account for one-sixth of all years lived with disability (YLDs) globally [ 1 ]. Additionally, an estimated 418 million disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) are attributed to mental illnesses [ 2 ]. The estimated cost of psychiatric diseases was US$2.5 trillion in 2010 and is expected to exceed US$6.0 trillion by 2030. The indirect monetary effects include diminished production and resources, unemployment, missed work, and premature death [ 3 ]. A significant portion of people (31.7%) with significant mental health conditions experience long-term disability and dependency [ 4 ]. Psychotropic medications are drugs that affect brain function, altering mood, perception, or behavior, and are used to treat psychiatric conditions such as depression, anxiety, bipolar disorder, schizophrenia, and Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD). These medications include antidepressants, antipsychotics, anxiolytics, mood stabilizers, stimulants, and sedative-hypnotics. They are prescribed based on the specific condition and require careful monitoring due to potential side effects [ 5 , 6 ]. Selecting the most appropriate medication can be challenging due to the wide range of options available, which underscores the importance of robust evidence. Psychotropic drugs have improved clinical outcomes for individuals with mental illnesses by effectively managing their symptoms [ 7 , 8 ]. Managing significant mental illnesses requires medication compliance, which can be difficult to achieve [ 9 – 11 ]. Several studies, including one from a population-based cohort of Ethiopian individuals with schizophrenia, have shown that medication adherence is associated with improved clinical outcomes and reduced mortality [ 12 , 13 ]. According to the WHO, medication non-adherence is defined as ‘any situation in which an individual’s medication-taking behavior diverges from established guidelines from medical providers’ [ 14 ]. Globally, over 50% of medications are not taken as prescribed, and more than half of patients use their medications inappropriately [ 15 ]. Across the world, therapy is in short supply and of poor quality, as evidenced by the fact that only one-third of individuals with depression and 29% of those with psychosis [ 16 ] receive formal mental health treatment [ 17 ]. A recent systematic review and meta-analysis across the world revealed that nearly half (49%) of people with mental illnesses were non-adherent psychotropic medications [ 18 ]. A cross-sectional study in Nigeria found that at least one in two (51.0%) outpatients with schizophrenia did not adhere to their prescribed antipsychotics [ 19 ]. Similarly, in Uganda, the prevalence of psychotropic medication non-adherence was estimated at 46.21% [ 20 ]. On the other hand, the prevalence rate of non-adherence to psychotropic drugs across the world was as low as 6% to as high as 65% [ 21 ]. People with significant mental illnesses are more likely to refrain from taking their prescribed medications due to inadequate understanding of their condition and how it is managed [ 22 – 24 ]. Patients who experience severe side effects more likely to be non-adherent compared to those who experience mild or no side effects [ 21 ]. Medication side effects are frequently cited as a reason for non-adherence, as they can cause discomfort, reduced quality of life, or raise concerns about long-term health [ 18 ]. In one study, approximately one-fourth of individuals reported experiencing tiredness, poor sleep quality, and weight gain [ 25 ]. Moreover, commonly reported reasons of non-adherence include forgetting to take medications and only taking drugs when individuals feel uncomfortable [ 26 , 27 ]. For instance, in one study, more than half of the subjects reported frequently forgetting to take their prescribed medication [ 28 ]. Adherence can be severely affected by a lack of social support and familial issues. Individuals without adequate social support are more likely to disregard their medications [ 29 – 32 ]. Another factor is the complexity of the drug regimen; individuals on simpler regimens are less likely to miss doses compared to those taking multiple doses per day [ 33 , 34 ]. Failure to follow prescribed therapies can result in worsening mental health problems or the recurrence of symptoms, reduce the effectiveness of treatment, and make individuals less receptive to future therapies [ 18 ]. This may lead to a higher demand for more intensive treatment, which could increase hospitalization rates and medical costs [ 35 ]. Patients who fail to adhere to prescribed treatments are at a greater risk of self-harm and suicidal thoughts [ 18 , 36 ]. Suicidal thoughts may stem from feelings of hopelessness and despair, which can be exacerbated by improper drug administration. Beyond clinical outcomes, non-adherence can also hinder an individual’s ability to perform daily tasks, such as maintaining a job, managing relationships, and self-care [ 37 ]. This can result lead in a general decline in quality of life, greater reliance on caregivers and social networks, and an increased risk of severe mental illnesses that are resistant to treatment. In severe cases, individuals may engage in behaviors leading to legal issues or homelessness, with instability caused by untreated symptoms playing a major role in these societal consequences [ 28 , 38 , 39 ]. Designing effective strategies to meet treatment goals for both patients and healthcare professionals requires research into the incidence of psychotropic drug non-adherence and factors that contribute to it in patients with serious mental disorders. Although numerous primary studies have been conducted in Ethiopia, there has been no systematic review or meta-analysis to aggregate information or guide policy on the issue. As a result, policymakers and program planners can benefit from a meta-analysis and systematic review that examines the magnitude and contributing factors of psychotropic drug non-adherence. Therefore, this study aims to assess the overall pooled estimated magnitude and determinants of psychotropic medication non-adherence among people living with mental illnesses in Ethiopia. Methods Protocol registration and development The International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO) has registered this systematic review and meta-analysis (ID: CRD42024563343) [ 40 ] and composed it in compliance with the criteria for Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Review and Meta-analysis (PRISMA) statements [Supplementary file 1 ]. Search strategies and method for identification of primary studies Based on the review question, the Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) and keywords have been generated. Search engines were used to look up studies from a variety of sources, including Google, and Google Scholar, as well as the primary electronic databases PubMed (Medline), EMBASE, CINAHL, Web of Science, and PsycINFO. A combination of the following MeSH phrases was used to generate search strings: “Psychotropic drugs” OR “psychotropic medications” OR “psychiatric drugs” OR “tranquilizers” OR “sedatives” OR “antidepressants” OR “mood altering drugs” OR “antipsychotics” AND “medications” OR “treatment” OR “drugs” AND “non-adherence” OR “adherence” OR “compliance” OR “non-compliance” OR “persistence” OR “retention” AND “determinants” OR “associated factors” OR “predictors” OR “influencing factors” OR “correlates” OR “barriers” OR “obstacles” OR “challenges” OR “contributing factors” OR “factors” OR “causes” OR “reasons” AND people living with mental illnesses” OR “severe mental illnesses” OR “psychiatric disorders” OR “mental illnesses” OR “mental disorders” OR “major depressive disorder” OR “schizophrenia” OR psychotic disorders” OR “psychosis” OR “anxiety disorders” OR “bipolar disorders” OR “mania” OR “depressive episodes” OR “ depression” OR “depressive symptoms” OR “persistent depressive disorder” OR “ Cyclothymic disorder” OR “dysthymic disorder” OR “ affective disorders” AND “Ethiopia”. Study setting The systematic review and meta-analysis included studies conducted exclusively in Ethiopia. Participants The study focused on people living with mental illnesses in Ethiopia, with particular emphasis on various demographic groups. Types of interventions/exposures Not applicable as this is an observational study, though the study focuses on psychotropic medication non-adherence and identification of associated factors. Comparators The study contrasts groups among people living with mental illnesses by comparing various sociodemographic and clinical factors that affect psychotropic medication non-adherence rates. Types of outcome measures The primary outcomes are the pooled prevalence and associated factors of psychotropic medication non-adherence among people living with mental illnesses in Ethiopia. Eligibility criteria Inclusion criteria This comprehensive systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to assess the prevalence of psychotropic medication non-adherence and its contributing factors among people living with mental illnesses in Ethiopia. The study included primary research on the prevalence and burden of psychotropic medication non-adherence. It focused on studies conducted among adults with mental illnesses such as major depressive disorder, schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, or anxiety disorder. Observational studies—including cross-sectional, comparative cross-sectional, case-control, and cohort designs—that reported the prevalence of psychotropic medication non-adherence and its contributing factors were considered. The selection process began with an initial assessment of the titles and abstracts of articles to determine eligibility. Subsequently, a thorough review of the full text was conducted to confirm the relevance of the study’s findings to this review. Two authors (SF and DD) independently reviewed each article for inclusion. Only original observational studies written in English and published online between June 11, 2024, and July 10, 2024, were included. Both published and unpublished studies meeting these criteria were considered. Finally, in this study, primary articles that were eligible for our review during the data extraction period were included, irrespective of their publication year. Exclusion criteria Studies were excluded if they were written in languages other than English, lacked an abstract or full text, or were qualitative, interventional, or observational studies that did not report the prevalence of psychotropic medication non-adherence. Additionally, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, expert opinions, case studies, case series, books, book chapters, brief reports, randomized controlled trials, and studies focused on therapy, follow-up, drug or clinical decision-making, or those with insufficient data to calculate prevalence were excluded. Data extraction Two authors of the study, SF and DD, independently extracted all the necessary data from the articles using a standardized data extraction format between June 11, 2024, and July 10, 2024.The data extraction template included key items such as, the first author’s name, publication year, study region, number of participants, screening tools used to assess psychotropic medication non-adherence, prevalence rates, and associated factors. The characteristics of the included articles were documented in Microsoft Word [Table 1 ], while the raw data on non-adherence and its contributing factors were organized in a Microsoft Excel spreadsheet (2010) [Supplementary file 2 ].
